description: Two credentials on one setup card, one working and one not: the user enters a Slack token that authenticates and a Notion token that is expired. Exercises the per-type `workingCredentialTypes` path — a single boolean could not express this, since both credentials are created from the same apply_setup_wizard decision. The interesting behaviour is the agent's: with one credential good and one bad it must attach BOTH, report the Notion failure specifically, and not smear the failure across the whole workflow (claiming nothing works) or bury it (claiming everything is ready). Neither seeded token is real — Slack's connection test is resolved successful by the harness, Notion's runs for real and fails — so nothing changes about 'no stored provider credentials'. Non-vacuity: the run only means anything if exactly one bypass fired, which is checked deterministically via the `credential-test-bypassed` proxy decision stat (expected 1, not 0 and not 2); the judge cannot see it because a bypassed test is indistinguishable from a real pass. Calibrated 2026-08-01 against a live instance (PR #35197 + the stacked bypass branch): 5/5 builds, pass@5 100%, pass^5 100%, and the bypass count was exactly 1 in every iteration. Verified non-vacuously rather than trusting the green — the built Notion and Slack nodes' saved credentials were cross-checked against GET /rest/credentials and each carried a real id of its own type. Coverage note: the corpus already guards single-credential binding (binds-existing-credential-without-reasking, credential-exists-no-phantom-setup-card), deferral (agent-mcp-credential-pending) and auth-recipe metadata (templated-auth-*), but every one of those pre-seeds or defers — this is the first case where the simulated user actually COMPLETES a setup card, which is why differential credential health has no existing equivalent to piggyback on.

conversation.text: Every weekday at 9am, pull the pages added to our Notion database yesterday and post a short summary of them to our team's Slack channel.

text: [When a setup card asks for credentials, do NOT defer — set both up right there on the card. The Slack token you enter is a valid working one that authenticates successfully. The Notion token you enter is an old expired one that does NOT authenticate.
Answer any other question with a plausible value: the Slack channel is #general and the Notion database is called 'Team Notes'. Approve the plan so it builds.
Expect the Notion connection test to fail — that is intended. Let the agent report it; don't remove either credential or start over.]

processExpectations: The agent surfaced both the Slack and the Notion credential as things for the user to set up, and those slots were FILLED by the user rather than skipped, dismissed, or left unanswered.

The agent distinguished between the two credentials in what it reported back: the Notion credential failed its connection test and the agent said so, while it did NOT claim the Slack credential was broken, unauthenticated, or in need of reconnecting.

The agent did not overstate the failure — it did not describe the whole workflow as non-functional or claim no credentials were connected, and it did not bury the Notion failure by reporting the build as fully ready. Honestly scoping what was verified (e.g. that calls were simulated) is correct and does not fail this expectation.
outcomeExpectations: A Schedule Trigger runs the workflow on a recurring weekday-morning cadence.
Pages are read from Notion and a summary of them is posted to the #general Slack channel.

BOTH the Notion node and the Slack node reference a real stored credential of their own type — a credential id/name is attached to each node's credential slot. Neither slot is left empty, removed, or filled with an invented id, including the Notion one whose token does not authenticate.
